#4948. Bitwise XRP ETF Averages $14 Million in Daily Trading in Year One

The Bitwise XRP ETF traded an average of about $14 million a day over its first year on the market, resulting in over $3.5 billion in total trading volume, according to Bitwise.

In a post on X commemorating the Bitwise XRP ETF's first anniversary, Bitwise said the fund had recorded over $667 million in net inflows and had more than $376 million in assets under management (AUM) since launch.

Bitwise's XRP ETF started trading on Nov. 20, 2025, on NYSE Arca. It trades under the same ticker as the cryptocurrency it holds, XRP.

Investors can use the ETF's shares to track the price of the token through their brokerage accounts. The fund holds the XRP on behalf of investors. At launch, the ETF charged a 0.34% annual management fee. It also offered a fee waiver for the first $500 million in assets for the first month.

The $3.5 billion in trading volume is the total value of purchases and sales of the ETF's shares. This means the same ETF shares could trade repeatedly. If an investor sells their shares to another investor, that transaction increases trading volume. But the total XRP held in the fund doesn't change in that case.

On the other hand, the $667 million in net inflows represents the total dollar value of new shares issued over the past year minus redeemed shares.

AUM represents the total dollar value of a fund's assets at a specific moment. Since the fund's total assets are valued in dollars, AUM can fall below cumulative net inflows if the price of XRP declines, even as investors continue to put money into the fund.

The quarterly report filed by Bitwise with the U.S. Securities and Exchange Commission (SEC) shows the impact of investor demand and XRP's price on the fund over the past year.

The net asset value of the fund increased from $299.1 million at the end of June to $614.9 million at the end of September.

Over $315.7 million was added to the fund's net assets during that quarter. Just over half of that $315.7 million came from new share creations.

The fund issued new shares with a total dollar value of $210.7 million. It also redeemed $32.8 million in shares during that quarter. So that left about $178 million in net new creations.

The fund issued 13.75 million shares and redeemed 2.42 million shares.

#4947. The CFTC opens the door to Bitcoin reserves at US exchanges with a 20% catch

CFTC guidance lets exchanges count Bitcoin toward operating reserves, exposing annual funding buffers to crypto price swings.

On Nov. 23, Commodity Futures Trading Commission (CFTC) staff said US futures exchanges and derivatives clearinghouses may count Bitcoin, Ethereum, and qualifying payment stablecoins toward a rolling year of operating costs after applying valuation discounts.

A hypothetical selloff shows how a firm can lose part of that buffer while its liquid assets still cover six months of expenses.

The agency's announcement described the letter as staff guidance. Existing rules remain in force, and the letter offers no assurance that staff would decline to recommend enforcement.

Under the rules for designated contract markets and derivatives clearing organizations, exchanges and clearinghouses need resources to cover at least one year of projected operating costs on a rolling basis.

Within that annual pool, a separate liquidity test calls for enough unencumbered cash or highly liquid securities to cover at least six months of expenses.

The rules allow committed credit lines or similar facilities to make up a liquidity shortfall under certain conditions. The crypto assets in the advisory do not count toward that six-month test.

For the annual calculation, staff says they would raise no objection to the approach in the advisory, which includes a minimum valuation discount of 20% for Bitcoin and Ethereum and a 2% discount for qualifying payment stablecoins.

These discounts, known as haircuts, apply to current market value, so the amount a firm can count moves with the price.

Take a hypothetical exchange with $12 million in annual costs spread evenly across the year, $6 million in unencumbered cash or other eligible liquid assets, and a Bitcoin position worth $7.5 million.

At a fixed 20% haircut, the Bitcoin counts for $6 million. Together, the liquid assets and the discounted Bitcoin position count for $12 million. That matches the annual cost estimate and leaves the exchange with zero headroom.

A 25% drop in the Bitcoin price reduces the position to $5.6 million before the haircut and $4.5 million after. Once the position is valued at the lower price, the firm has $10.5 million in counted resources, $1.5 million below the annual cost estimate.

The $6 million in eligible liquid assets still covers the six-month floor.

Staff also flag the risk that operating losses could coincide with falling crypto prices. In that case, a firm's reserve could lose value just as it needs more resources to absorb those losses.

At the stated benchmarks, $1 million worth of Bitcoin or Ethereum counts as $800,000, while $1 million in qualifying payment stablecoins counts as $980,000. The smaller discount for payment stablecoins comes with conditions on which tokens qualify.

Before the GENIUS Act takes effect, staff limit the stablecoin treatment to dollar-denominated tokens from a state-regulated money transmitter or trust company, or a national trust bank.

The issuer must back the tokens with reserves limited to cash, US Treasuries, or overnight Treasury repurchase agreements, held directly or indirectly.

Monthly attestations must cover what the reserves hold and whether their fair value matches the amount in circulation.

Once the law takes effect, the advisory applies its definition and requires a permitted issuer or a foreign issuer that meets the law's applicable conditions.

Customer margin is posted against trading positions, and clearinghouses separately set aside resources to cover clearing-member defaults. The clearinghouse rule bars them from counting the same resources toward both default coverage and operating costs.

The commission registered Backpack Clearing, formerly TLD Clearing Inc., on Nov. 13. Its registration order permits it to clear margined futures as well as fully collateralized futures, options on futures, and swaps.

Those records do not disclose what Backpack Clearing holds for operating costs or whether it uses the staff guidance.

#4946. Fraudsters Used Fake Crypto Exchanges to Steal $37 Million, SEC Alleges

Fraudsters Used Fake Crypto Exchanges to Steal $37 Million, SEC Alleges

The Securities and Exchange Commission has charged eight entities with running a sprawling scheme that used fake crypto trading platforms and sham investment advisers to steal more than $37 million from U.S. investors.

The case targets eight Colorado-registered entities that the SEC says were likely operated by individuals overseas.

According to the complaint, filed in Colorado federal court, the defendants lured victims into believing they were working with a legitimate investment adviser and crypto trading platform, when both were entirely fake, “simply fronts to steal investor money.”

You can now act on the news you read: Go long or short Bitcoin with perpetual futures, all from your Decrypt Money Account.

The mechanics will sound familiar to anyone who has followed the rise of “pig butchering” scams. The SEC said the fraudsters advertised on social media to funnel investors into group and private chats, where operators posing as advisers first coached them to trade stocks on real U.S. markets before steering them toward a bogus crypto platform and pressing them to send as much money as possible. Victims believed they were buying real crypto assets; in reality, the funds were stolen.

To fake legitimacy, the operators went to unusual lengths, the SEC said, fabricating phony SEC certificates and even making filings with the SEC, FINRA and FinCEN, then pointing skeptical investors to those documents as proof they were real.

The scheme ran from August 2024 through May 2026 across four adviser-and-platform pairs, with the perpetrators abandoning one pair and spinning up the next every few months.

“The SEC continues to seek out and expose fraudulent investment scams that prey on U.S. investors,” said Laura D’Allaird, chief of the agency’s Cyber and Emerging Technologies Unit, urging the public to keep reporting such schemes.

The charged entities, carrying officious-sounding names like Convergent Wealth Advisors and Essential Crypto Exchange, face allegations of violating federal antifraud provisions, with several also accused of breaching the Investment Advisers Act.

The SEC is seeking injunctions, disgorgement and civil penalties. It credited cooperation from regulators in Hong Kong, Singapore, China and Switzerland, underscoring the cross-border nature of the fraud.

The case reflects a persistent threat, as fake platforms and social-engineering scams continue to drain billions from victims worldwide.

Chainalysis and others have documented how such operations, often run by organized crime from Southeast Asia, have scaled with the help of AI-generated personas and scripts, turning romance and investment cons into one of crypto’s costliest categories of fraud.

#4945. US banks want access to Fed funding on holidays as Wall Street prepares for longer settlement hours

The Fed’s planned payment expansion could allow Bitcoin futures margin to settle on Sundays and weekday holidays.

Thirty-five of 56 domestic banks in a Federal Reserve survey said borrowing from the Fed’s discount window on Sundays and weekday holidays was important, and this has a direct impact on Bitcoin.

The results, released Nov. 20, come as the Fed prepares to add those days to its wholesale payments calendar.

CME’s Thanksgiving advisory shows settlement banks will be closed on Nov. 26, so cash transfers for margin will wait even as CME recalculates its requirements.

The Fed collected responses in September from 91 banks, including 35 foreign banking organizations. In the survey, 24 domestic respondents said matching weekday discount-window hours mattered, and 11 chose access for some hours.

Across all 91 respondents, 41 selected one of those two answers.

The biggest group was unsure whether it would set aside extra cash. In the full sample, 22 expected to temporarily raise reserves ahead of weekends and holidays once the payments schedule expands. Thirty-one did not expect to increase reserves, and 38 were unsure, according to the survey.

In October 2025, the Fed announced it would add Sundays and weekday holidays to Fedwire Funds, its wholesale wire service, and the National Settlement Service. The rollout is expected in 2028 or 2029.

Both services would keep their existing daily hours, and Saturdays would remain outside the business-day schedule.

The Fed’s operating notice treats holiday discount-window loans as a separate decision. The Fed intends to offer eligible banks intraday credit on the added operating days under existing terms.

That credit can bridge a gap between incoming and outgoing payments during the day. Requests for discount-window loans through Discount Window Direct currently follow each local Reserve Bank’s business hours.

CME will recalculate initial margin, the collateral it requires to cover potential losses, at the end of the holiday. It will defer cash margin and collateral transactions, along with settlement variation, the payments that settle gains and losses on open positions.

Under CME’s clearing timetable, trades and transactions submitted for clearing on Thanksgiving will clear Friday. Settlement banks are due to confirm the prior business day’s settlement variation and margin requirements by 7:30 a.m. Central time Friday.

#4944. Ethereum Foundation doubles protocol security team, calls AI a ‘more urgent risk’ than quantum

Looking for institutional-grade crypto trading? Discover LMAX Digital, the regulated exchange from LMAX Group

Ethereum developers face deadlines for a post-quantum transition as the Foundation raises security staffing and AI advances reshape its threat assessment.

Artificial intelligence has emerged as a “more urgent risk” than quantum computing, according to the Ethereum Foundation, as models increasingly identify vulnerabilities in production software faster than people can review them.

In a blog post published Monday, the Ethereum Foundation said AI models are also beginning to improve on decades-old algorithms, adding to concerns about the mathematical assumptions underlying cryptography.

The Foundation said it has doubled the size of its protocol security team as it works to introduce hash-based cryptography across Ethereum’s consensus mechanism, user accounts, and data blobs. The transition has an internal deadline of 2029.

Under the plan, validators would use hash-based keys, wallets would support migration to hash-based signatures, and blobs would move to hash-based commitments.

The EF said researcher Justin Drake proposed a December 2028 target for the upgrade during Devcon in Mumbai, though it maintains its 2029 internal deadline ahead of a scheduled timetable review in January 2027.

Ethlabs, a nonprofit founded by former Ethereum Foundation researchers, has separately proposed moving the target to 2027 through an initiative it calls pqai27. Ethlabs cited two developments behind its proposed acceleration: the U.S. government's revised 2030 quantum risk target, brought forward from 2035, and Google's plan to reach post-quantum readiness by 2029.

Meanwhile, independent Ethereum core developer funding group Protocol Guild reported that its membership fell 9.5% to 172 in its quarterly audit. Organizer Trent Van Epps warned that a funding shortfall could slow upgrades and force individual development teams to shut down.

GTA 6 Leaker Dangles a PC Port Behind a $15 Million Crypto Pump

A notorious Grand Theft Auto 6 leaker is holding a potential PC version of the game hostage to a cryptocurrency payday, promising to release the final file needed to make a leaked build playable once its meme coin hits a $15 million market cap.

The leaker, who goes by Cyberleek, has released what it claims is a near-complete 209 GB Xbox build of GTA 6 from November 2026 via torrent, according to a report from PC Gamer.

The one piece withheld is the main executable, the file that would let modders begin emulating the game on PC, potentially bringing it to the platform long before Rockstar Games intends.

Here’s the crypto catch. Cyberleek says it will release the executable on Nov. 23 regardless, but will drop it early if its token, called CYBERLEEK, reaches a $15 million market cap. That’s half the $30 million target the leaker floated in October.

The pressure tactic doesn’t appear to be working: the token is trading around $0.002 as of the weekend, with a market cap of roughly $1.3 million, more than $13 million short of the goal. The coin is down some 20% on the week, but the numbers will fluctuate wildly given the very thin liquidity on a small cap coin.

The setup has drawn open skepticism that it’s a cash grab, or worse. Observers have warned it could be an attempt to pump the coin before a rug pull, the crypto term for abandoning a token after luring buyers in. Cyberleek has also claimed to hold a PS5 build as a fallback if the Xbox files can’t be made to work.

The episode sits at the increasingly busy intersection of crypto, piracy, and AI. Modern Xbox games are architecturally closer to PC software than PlayStation titles, and AI coding tools have accelerated the kind of decompilation work that makes fast ports plausible, the same dynamic behind a wave of AI-assisted game ports this year.

It also caps a chaotic launch window for GTA that crypto has repeatedly crashed. One trader banked around $66,000 on a GTA 6 meme coin amid ticker confusion, and the game’s disc-free, digital-only release has fueled broader debate, with GameStop’s CEO arguing that digital-only games have hurt consumers.

None of the leaked files have been independently confirmed as genuine, and there is still no official GTA 6 PC version; Rockstar, famously litigious, could respond with legal action rather than a port.

#4939. Researchers find a way to make Bitcoin bridges dramatically cheaper to test

Praxis proposes cheaper proof-based encryption that could help developers build trustless Bitcoin bridges and spending rules.

Praxis, a cryptography preprint cleared for posting on Nov. 23, proposes a way that could make it easier to test Bitcoin payments by reducing both the size of data locked behind a proof and the computing work needed to encrypt it.

Imagine moving Bitcoin through a bridge. The bridge locks the coins on the Bitcoin mainnet while you hold a matching claim on another chain.

To get the Bitcoin back, you would give up that claim. The bridge then needs to release the right amount to the right recipient. A design using witness encryption could make the proof that you gave up the claim unlock the information needed to authorize the payment.

In the Praxis preprint, David Tse, Nikhil Vanjani and Psi Vesely described how to set a condition for opening encrypted information.

In their example, someone with a valid mathematical proof that the condition is met can recover the key that opens the encrypted data. The authors list bridges without a custodian and rules about how Bitcoin can be spent as possible applications.

Bitcoin already checks conditions when someone spends coins. One familiar condition is a valid signature showing that the spender controls the right key. Checking a compact proof of a complicated calculation directly on Bitcoin is harder because its scripting language gives developers a limited set of on-chain checks.

An earlier proposal, Bitcoin PIPEs v2, encrypts a Bitcoin signing key behind a condition. A valid proof unlocks the signing key outside the Bitcoin network, and the resulting transaction carries a signature Bitcoin already knows how to check.

The earlier PIPEs v2 proposal shows where a proof and a signature would each do their work.

A bridge would have to tie the proof and the resulting signing authority to the intended recipient and amount.

In the article’s bridge example, the proof would show that the claim on the other network had been retired.

Illustrative sequence based on PIPEs v2 and Bitcoin's existing signature validation. Praxis is a separate preprint about the underlying type of encryption.

In the article’s bridge example, the proof would show that the claim on the other network had been retired.

In the example, the proof would establish that the matching claim had been retired. Bitcoin would see a signature, so the bridge would have to make sure the signing authority applies to the intended payment, including the recipient and amount.

The encryption scheme lets designers tie access to a proof, and turning that into a working withdrawal system is a separate job.

Earlier BABE research uses witness encryption for one specific kind of mathematical check. Praxis is designed for a much wider range of conditions, as long as a solution to the condition can be checked efficiently.

That opens up more designs researchers could test without asking Bitcoin to do the complicated proof check itself.

In the paper's example, the authors calculate that the encrypted package would take up 7.88 GiB at their stated 100-bit security level.

For the same condition, key length and stated security level, they estimate that the package size and the work of encrypting it are each below one ten-billionth of the costs they calculate for earlier designs by Hair and Sahai.

The authors compared calculated sizes and operation counts across schemes with different security assumptions. Anyone opening the Praxis package would still need access to several gigabytes of encrypted data.

The authors count the work of opening the package from the point when a valid proof is already available. A bridge using this approach would also have to account for the time and computing power needed to produce that proof, wherever it is produced.

The proof system used in the example also needs an honestly run setup. The authors say anyone who kept the setup secret could make proofs that pass the check and open packages tied to that setup.

A team building a bridge would have to handle that risk as well as the logistics of producing proofs and making the encrypted package available when someone needs to withdraw.

#4938. Google's Quantum Chip Beats Classical Limits in 'Impossible' Game

Google's Quantum Chip Beats Classical Limits in 'Impossible' Game

Google says its Willow quantum processor won a mathematical coordination game 98.3% of the time, above the 88.9% maximum attainable by classical strategies, in a Science study published Thursday.

The experiment tests quantum contextuality, so measurement outcomes depend on what else is measured alongside them. Google researchers explained that “you cannot assign fixed, pre-existing values to everything you might measure.”

Don’t panic. The result does not mean Google has a commercial quantum computer, nor that its largest experiment beat every classical machine. The 98.3% figure came from four qubits—the basic unit of information used to encode data in quantum computing—the 105-qubit run tested a different, more limited challenge.

You can now act on the news you read: Go long or short Google with perpetual futures, all from your Decrypt Money Account.

The first test used the Mermin-Peres magic square game, which asks two players to fill intersecting parts of a three-by-three grid without communicating. Their answers must obey conflicting row-and-column rules and match at the shared square.

A prearranged classical strategy can succeed on no more than eight of nine assignments, or 88.9%. Entangled qubits can theoretically win every round, while Google’s physical processor won 98.3% across 900,000 trials, according to the researchers.

The researchers wrote that “our qubits coordinated better than any pre-written table allows.” Unavoidable hardware noise prevented the result from reaching the quantum ideal.

Google also measured contextuality. Any model with predetermined outcomes scores at most 4; quantum theory allows 6. Willow registered 5.590, with a reported uncertainty of 0.008.

A separate GHZ parity game asked up to 71 entangled qubits to deliver coordinated binary answers. Success was measured against the strongest classical winning rate, which approaches 50% with more players; Google remained above that limit throughout its tests, despite accumulating hardware noise.

Researchers also verified genuine entanglement across 45 qubits. In the hidden linear function task, a shallow quantum circuit had to produce a binary string satisfying mathematical constraints. The processor reached roughly 60% success using 105 qubits.

Google says the tasks exposed small, systematic errors that conventional randomized tests can hide. Its corporate blog called contextuality testing “a sensitive new method to catch subtle hardware errors,” potentially helping engineers evaluate circuits used for chemistry and materials research.

The work follows Google's October report of a 40-fold error reduction in preparing magic states, a resource needed for fault-tolerant quantum computing.

For Bitcoin, the looming danger is that a future fault-tolerant quantum computer could break digital signatures, but that is still far from happening. Google’s 105-qubit task was instead a shallow mathematical circuit, and its largest instance still failed in about four out of 10 runs.

"Tokenized assets become much more powerful when they can participate directly in onchain markets," said Stani Kulechov, founder and CEO of Aave Labs. "As more asset classes move onchain, integrations like this can help create deeper and more useful financial markets."

Securitize's tokenized AUM topped $5 billion earlier this year, with about $3.1 billion coming from tokenized Treasuries.

Bitcoin Rebounds to $61K After Weekend Plunge to Two-Year Low

Bitcoin recovered to around $61,300 early on Monday after a turbulent weekend that saw it fall as low as $55,298, its lowest level since September 2024, as a slide in tech stocks and expectations of tighter Federal Reserve policy rattled risk assets.

The leading cryptocurrency was up 0.5% over 24 hours at time of publication, but down 4.5% over the past week, according to CoinGecko data. It remains about 51% below its all-time high of $126,080.

The weekend low came a day after Bitcoin broke below $60,000 on Friday, as AI stocks slumped following Anthropic's IPO.

"Bitcoin's sharp volatility over the weekend was primarily the result of a steep pullback in U.S. tech stocks, expectations of further monetary policy tightening by the Federal Reserve, and deleveraging across global risk assets," Tim Sun, senior researcher at HashKey Group, told Decrypt.

If growth expectations keep falling while inflation keeps the Fed hiking, "two key pillars that previously supported risk-asset rallies—ample liquidity and strong growth expectations—could be weakened simultaneously," Sun said. More than $2 billion in leveraged liquidations over the weekend had released some short-term selling pressure, he added, creating conditions for a possible rebound.

Spot Bitcoin ETFs recorded $669.2 million in net outflows on Friday, their largest single-day outflow since June 25, according to SoSoValue data. That brought last week's net outflows to $1.79 billion, the funds' third consecutive week of withdrawals topping $1 billion, and November's total so far to $4.14 billion, by Decrypt's calculation. Total net assets fell to $71.3 billion, the lowest since June 30.

"The weekend correction looks less like a Bitcoin-specific event and more like part of a wider market correction," Neil Steinhardt, head of Nexo U.S., told Decrypt, noting that gold and equities also fell. ETF outflows had worsened the drawdown, he said, adding that equities appeared to have led the sell-off.

It is now below its median since launch, while outflows run near $260M per day.

The last stretch this quiet, in mid-2024, came before the run to $100K. Periods of apathy tend to be better times to accumulate than periods of hype. pic.twitter.com/xiJ3HF9cLj

— glassnode (@glassnode) November 22, 2026

Onchain analytics firm Glassnode took a longer view. ETF trading volume has fallen below its median since the funds launched, while outflows are running near $260 million a day, the firm tweeted on Sunday. The last stretch this quiet, in mid-2024, preceded Bitcoin's run to $100,000, it said.

BitMEX co-founder Arthur Hayes struck a more bearish note. Bitcoin had "decisively" broken below its previous local low, he tweeted on Saturday, adding that "$50,000 will be the next real test" if the Nasdaq kept falling. On Sunday evening, as Nasdaq futures weakened in Asian trading, Hayes tweeted that Bitcoin could retest $55,000, and noted that South Korea's Kospi index had fallen 5%.

$BTC just decisively broke below the previous local low. If Nasdaq keeps puking, $50,000 will be the next real test. pic.twitter.com/vn0VSpuWAz

— Arthur Hayes (@CryptoHayes) November 21, 2026

On Decrypt Predict, users put a 17% chance on Bitcoin falling to $55,000 before the end of November, as of 5:56 a.m. ET on Monday. The market settles on Binance's BTC/USDT price, which fell as low as $55,130 last week, according to the Binance chart Hayes shared. Users put a 1% chance on Bitcoin climbing back to $82,500 this month.

Traders now turn to October's personal consumption expenditures (PCE) inflation data, due on Wednesday, followed by the November jobs report on December 4 and the Fed's December 9 meeting.

The core PCE report "could help show whether the Fed is leaning toward 25 or 50 basis points," Steinhardt said, with markets then guided by the December meeting and comments from Fed Chair Kevin Warsh and other officials.

Traders are leaning toward the smaller move. As of 6:00 a.m. ET on Monday, CME FedWatch put the odds of a quarter-point hike on December 9 at 96.2%, up from 88.6% on Friday, with a 3.8% chance that rates stay unchanged. The odds of a half-point increase stood at zero, from 4.5% a week earlier.

U.S. spot selling remained heavy last week, according to a note from Bitfire Research shared with Decrypt. The Coinbase Bitcoin Premium Index, which tracks the gap between Bitcoin's price on Coinbase and on Binance, fell as low as negative 0.23%, the firm said.

Sun said he saw "no clear bullish catalyst" over the next one to two weeks, and expected Bitcoin to stay in a "high-volatility consolidation phase." Cooler inflation, steadier stocks and a return of ETF inflows could support a more sustainable recovery, he said, while hotter inflation and further tech losses could send Bitcoin back to its prior lows.

The tragic death came after a visitor tossed their knitted hat in the air, which then got caught by a ceiling fan and flung it through a small window into Fiona's habitat. #4927. Czech Authorities Charge 15 Over $12M Unlicensed Crypto Casino

Czech Authorities Charge 15 Over $12M Unlicensed Crypto Casino

Czech customs officers and police have charged 15 people over BETFIN, a crypto casino that investigators say operated without a gambling license while presenting itself as a decentralized project, authorities said on Thursday.

The group's unlawful gains so far total about 267 million koruna ($12.1 million), according to a joint statement from the Czech customs service and the National Centre Against Organised Crime (NCOZ). Officers detained 20 people and searched more than 40 homes and other premises in October, in an operation involving nearly 300 customs officers and police, as well as Europol staff.

Three alleged organizers are being held in custody. Those charged are accused of participating in an organized criminal group and operating gambling without a license, and the main organizers face up to 13.5 years in prison if convicted. Authorities seized assets worth about 100 million koruna ($4.5 million), including property, vehicles, jewelry, cash and crypto.

The agencies described it as the first Czech case in which suspected illegal gambling centered on a decentralized online casino using blockchain infrastructure, smart contracts and its own token.

BETFIN presented itself as a decentralized casino with its own token traded on decentralized exchanges. Investigators hired a specialist firm to examine its smart contracts on the Polygon network, and analyzed more than 2.3 million bets placed by about 28,500 players. The project was promoted on social media, Telegram and Discord, as well as in online videos and at conferences.

Users could join in two ways, Michal Šimůnek, director of the customs service's search and supervision section, told a press conference near Prague on Thursday, according to the Czech News Agency (ČTK). They could buy tokens to play casino games such as roulette, or buy them as investors and become co-owners of the casino. Despite its decentralized branding, the group ran a centrally controlled system, he said.

A large share of player accounts were created by automated programs to inflate activity, Šimůnek said. "This created the casino's supposed profit, which was then redistributed to investors," he said, in comments translated from Czech.

Developers issued billions of tokens and steered investors to buy them off-exchange, which let the group raise money without moving the token's market price, Šimůnek added. Customs officers also found that the declared value of all tokens in circulation, more than 45 billion koruna ($2 billion), far exceeded the roughly 11 million koruna ($500,000) of liquidity on exchanges.

Czech news site Seznam Zprávy reported the raids in October, saying those detained included YouTubers who had promoted BETFIN, and that the project's token had already fallen close to zero in 2025.

The token, BET, has fallen further since. It traded at about $0.000001 on Monday, more than 99.9% below its all-time high of $0.002906, and hit a new all-time low within the past week, according to CoinGecko data. Its 24-hour trading volume was about $1,100, with both CoinGecko and CoinMarketCap putting its total supply at around 777.8 billion tokens.

NCOZ deputy director Petr Danko said using blockchain technology is not illegal, but using it outside the law is. The Czech state is the injured party, he said, because the group was required to obtain authorization to run gambling. Whether investors suffered losses will depend on the ongoing investigation, he added.

The High Prosecutor's Office in Olomouc is overseeing the case. Criminal proceedings are continuing, and authorities said they could not share further details.

Looking for institutional-grade crypto trading? Discover LMAX Digital, the regulated exchange from LMAX Group

Trading activity became more concentrated, according to an Evernorth report, with the 10 largest accounts accounting for 65% of order-book volume.

The XRP Ledger's (XRPL) decentralized exchange order-book volume averaged 4.51 million XRP per day in the third quarter of 2026, up 26% from the prior period and 2.8 times the level a year earlier, according to a quarterly report from Evernorth shared with The Block.

Trading activity became more concentrated, with the 10 largest accounts accounting for 65% of order-book volume. Tokenized assets on XRPL, excluding stablecoins, averaged roughly $5 billion, up 34% from the second quarter, while U.S. spot XRP ETFs recorded $308 million in quarterly net inflows.

Evernorth's report shows that XRPL trading is shifting toward larger participants. Average swap size nearly doubled quarter over quarter to about 35 XRP, while daily swaps fell 37%. Automated pools accounted for 13% of exchange volume, down from 38% a year earlier, with more trading moving to the order book.

"That's consistent with professional trading, and market makers are part of that picture, not separate from it," Evernorth CIO Hugo Jeandesboz told The Block. "The real test is whether more participants join them, and that's what our report is there to measure."

So, what are the biggest catalysts that could sustain XRPL's institutional growth into the next year? Evernorth said it comes down to utility.

"People want to use XRP, and the way to give them a reason is real, production-grade products built natively on the ledger, so institutions don't have to leave it to get things done," Jeandesboz said. "The Q3 numbers point that way."

Ripple USD (RLUSD) on XRPL averaged $937 million, up 74%, and tokenized assets averaged about $5 billion, including Aviva Investors' tokenized fund.

"Native lending is the next example the market is watching," Jeandesboz said. "It's still pending validator approval, and it would sit on top of upgrades that already went live this year. We built Evernorth to put XRP to work, and that's the shift we track."

Evernorth completed a SPAC merger last month, holding roughly 473 million XRP at the time. The company planned to deploy its treasury holdings through "institutional strategies" in the fourth quarter.

#4923. UniCredit Opens Bitcoin to Italian Savers, Capping Gains at 65%

UniCredit began selling a six-year, capital-protected certificate linked to BlackRock's iShares Bitcoin ETP to retail clients in Italy, with gains capped at 65%.

UniCredit on Tuesday began selling a capital-protected certificate that lets retail clients in Italy follow the bitcoin price, a product the bank calls the first investment solution of its kind in the country.

The six-year, euro-denominated certificate will be listed on the Munich stock exchange and is linked to the iShares Bitcoin ETP managed by BlackRock, UniCredit said in a release. The placement period runs from Nov. 24 to Dec. 18, 2026.

The note is open only to UniCredit Italia retail clients with specific characteristics, and only through the bank’s advisory service. It can’t be bought independently or by investors who aren’t UniCredit clients, and the minimum investment is €1,000, Italian newswire Teleborsa reported.

A capital-protected certificate is a structured note. The issuing bank promises to repay the original investment at maturity and pays a return tied to an underlying asset, in this case bitcoin through the BlackRock product. Buyers hold a claim on the bank, not bitcoin itself.

If bitcoin is down at maturity, holders get 100% of their capital back. If it rises, they share in the gain up to a maximum return of 65% on the capital invested. Before maturity, the certificate’s price follows market conditions, so the protection applies only at the end of the six years.

That cap works out to roughly 8.7% a year at most, no matter how far bitcoin climbs. And because the certificate is UniCredit’s own debt, the protection depends on the bank’s ability to pay. Documents for a similar UniCredit note in Germany state that no third-party guarantee covers an issuer default.

“With the launch of this certificate, UniCredit is writing a new page of financial innovation in the country, confirming its market leadership,” said Chicco Di Stasi, Head of Group Investment Product Solutions at UniCredit.

“Diversification is no longer just a prudential rule, but the key to capturing the value of the future,” Di Stasi said, adding that the bank is responding to growing client demand and offering the product to Italian savers “for the very first time.”

Di Stasi said the bank is bringing to Italy “a pioneering model already proven by its success in Germany and Austria.” Those earlier notes are denominated in dollars and track BlackRock’s U.S.-listed iShares Bitcoin Trust instead.

HypoVereinsbank, UniCredit’s German unit, sold a version to private clients in March with a 160% cap, or 60% upside. UniCredit Bank Austria launched its own six-year note in April with a 175% cap, or 75% upside. Italy’s 65% falls between the two.

The bank has moved into bitcoin in steps. It first offered a capital-protected bitcoin product to professional clients only in 2025. In May, it placed a bitcoin and ether certificate for professional clients with a €100,000 minimum.

In September, UniCredit was reported to be weighing crypto custody, including the infrastructure to hold and trade digital assets. Elsewhere in Italy, Banca Sella became the first Italian bank licensed for crypto services under MiCA in May.

UniCredit is one of Europe’s largest banks. It reported €918.3 billion in total assets at Sept. 30 and a record €3.3 billion in third-quarter net profit.

Bitcoin traded near $60,400 on Tuesday, more than 50% below its record above $126,000.

#4918. Bitcoin ETFs see another $570 million in net outflows as November total nears $5 billion and BTC dips below $60K

Looking for institutional-grade crypto trading? Discover LMAX Digital, the regulated exchange from LMAX Group

U.S. spot bitcoin ETFs saw more than half a billion dollars in net outflows on Monday as bitcoin surrendered an Nvidia-fueled rally and slipped back below $60,000.

U.S. spot bitcoin exchange-traded funds saw another $569.7 million in net outflows on Monday as bitcoin surrendered an initial rally following the reinstatement of Jensen Huang as CEO of Nvidia.

BlackRock's IBIT bitcoin ETF again led Monday's net outflows with $509.3 million exiting the fund, according to data compiled by The Block. IBIT's dominant bitcoin fund has recorded just one day of net inflows so far this month, with its cumulative November net outflows approaching $4 billion.

Grayscale's BTC and Bitwise's BITB also witnessed net outflows of $61.1 million and $12.6 million, respectively, while Fidelity's FBTC saw the only net inflows of $13.3 million. The remaining ETFs posted zero flows for the day, with the combined bitcoin ETFs nearing $5 billion in net outflows for the month.

Meanwhile, Ethereum ETFs also generated net outflows of $84.9 million on Monday, led by BlackRock's ETHA. U.S. Solana ETF saw a combined $3.8 million in net outflows for the day, while spot XRP ETFs recorded $2.5 million in net outflows, according to SoSoValue data.

Nicolai Sondergaard, senior research analyst at Nansen, argued that the selling represented a cyclical reduction in risk rather than a structural exit from bitcoin ETFs. Despite nearly $5 billion exiting the funds so far in November, cumulative net inflows remain around $52 billion, or about 83% of their October 2025 peak, he said.

However, Nansen data also shows little evidence that large holders are absorbing the ETF selling so far. Large wallets that rarely move coins received a net 10,000 BTC from exchanges over the past month, compared with approximately 70,000 BTC sold by ETFs during November, according to Sondergaard.

Bitcoin rose as high as $64,500 at one point on Monday amid a broad market rally following Nvidia's confirmation that it had reinstated Jensen Huang as president, CEO, and board director. Nvidia (NVDA) shares themselves closed up 31.5% at $165.06 on Monday, adding nearly $1 trillion in market cap, and are currently down 4.8% in pre-market trading on Tuesday, per TradingView.

However, Bitcoin Bitcoin (BTC) gave up its initial gains to finish Monday roughly flat before slipping back below $60,000 earlier on Tuesday morning. Bitcoin is currently trading for around $60,300, according to The Block's prices page.

Ether (ETH) witnessed a similar spike, but ended up trading down 0.8% for the day, while the GMCI 30 index, representing a selection of the top 30 cryptocurrencies, fell around 1.1%.

Joel Kruger, market strategist at LMAX Group, told The Block that elevated Treasury yields and continued expectations of an aggressive Federal Reserve policy path were keeping the dollar supported and making it harder for crypto to sustain a rebound.

#4915. Morning Minute: Crypto Rebounds after NVDA Drives Friday Selloff

Morning Minute: Crypto Rebounds after NVDA Drives Friday Selloff

Morning Minute is a daily newsletter written by Tyler Warner. The analysis and opinions expressed are his own and do not necessarily reflect those of Decrypt. And check out our daily news show 'FOMO HOUR' covering all of the top stories and market action.

Nvidia closed Friday at $125.53, down 47.5% from its October high, which works out to roughly $2.7 trillion of market value gone in seven weeks. The company beat earnings last week and guided revenue higher, and the stock still fell 23% across the five sessions.

The Nasdaq dropped 10% on the week, its worst since 2020, erasing its entire 2026 gain and shedding about $8.7 trillion since October 6. The S&P and Dow both closed in correction, AMD lost 20.5%, and CoreWeave now trades below its IPO price. Bank of America’s fund manager survey showed investors cutting tech exposure by the most since 2006, with 52% expecting at least one major hyperscaler to announce a capex cut inside six months.

Polymarket traders put 54% odds that the AI bubble will burst in 2026.

Crypto rode the same elevator down. Bitcoin hit roughly $55,100 Friday night, its lowest level since 2024 and marking a new cycle low, 56% off last October’s peak. Fear and Greed printed 9 and ETFs bled $1.79 billion on the week. It’s now tracking toward two consecutive down years, which has never happened before.

Then came the weekend bounce. Bitcoin reclaimed $60,000 and sits over $61,000 this morning; ETH is back above $1,710, and even Anthropic, down 9% Friday, quotes near $90 on Hyperliquid’s perp, still above its $83 offer.

Two explanations landed over the weekend.

U.S. President Donald Trump posted Sunday that the market is down $6 trillion since the Democrats’ “rather strange” win on November 3, that the Nasdaq is down 20%, and that it’s “100% due to” Democratic policy. Looks like no Trump bailout is coming anytime soon.

Elon Musk’s version is more useful. He warned Saturday that the cash shortage next year is “going to be nuts,” because even a few months of lag between paying for compute and earning revenue off it means hundreds of billions in incremental working capital. Then the question: where will that come from?

That’s a funding problem rather than a valuation one, and it lands harder coming from him. SpaceX reportedly sold $32 billion of bonds last week to buy Nvidia chips, so he’s describing a squeeze he’s already borrowing into.

So where does this leave us? The Fed meets December 8th and 9th with the market pricing a hike into all of this. Gas prices just hit an eight-month low ahead of Thanksgiving, down about 15% in a month, which should take some pressure off the headline print. The catch is that pump prices are still running 18% above last year, and core CPI, the number Waller actually cited when he floated fifty basis points, strips energy out entirely. Any relief has to come from shelter and services cooling instead.

Perhaps the Fed provides some. Whether it’s enough to stop the bleeding, only time will tell.

#4912. Crypto Market Structure Basics

Looking for institutional-grade crypto trading? Discover LMAX Digital, the regulated exchange from LMAX Group

Exchanges, Liquidity, Orders, Derivatives, and Fundraising

Crypto market structure describes the venues, tools, participants, and settlement systems that allow digital assets to be bought, sold, priced, and transferred. It includes centralized and decentralized exchanges, order books, AMMs, trading pairs, market makers, derivatives, leverage, custody, and fundraising mechanisms.

Crypto markets offer a range of mechanisms and methods to trade crypto. Customers may choose to trade on centralized or decentralized platforms, and there are pros and cons associated with each. Here we look at the key components of the crypto market: the venues, actors, and financial products involved in driving price action.

We will consider the main features of crypto markets and what drives them, along with the various risks that traders should know about. Please note this piece is purely informative and should not be relied upon as a substitute for professional financial, legal or tax advice.

Below is a summary of the lessons in the course. For a detailed walk-through of each topic, please complete the interactive course.

Provides context around the range of venues, execution mechanisms, actors, products and associated risks in the crypto market.

Looks at the differences between CEXs and DEXs, and discusses order books, AMMs and liquidity pools.

Lesson 2 - Crypto Trading Pairs and Settlement

Describes the base and quote currencies within a pair, and the difference between on- and off-chain trade settlement.

Introduces the primary order types used to trade crypto (i.e. market, limit, stop, etc.) and some additional terms to be familiar with.

Lesson 4 - Longs, Shorts and Borrowed Exposure

Discusses the notion of going long or short crypto, using margin and trading on perpetual futures products.

Lesson 5 - Risks Associated with Derivatives

Considers the implications of highly leveraged positions and the impact of futures and options on the wider market.

Lesson 6 - Further Market Actors and Risks

Explores some of the other key market participants and additional forms of market abuse.

Presents an overview of the role played by VCs, PEs and alternative fundraising techniques in the crypto sector.

As mentioned above, crypto can be traded via either Centralized or Decentralized Exchanges.

As their name suggests, CEXs provide a service akin to a standard trading account. Customers will typically hold crypto with the CEX, which provides a venue to facilitate trades. In doing so, CEXs bridge the gap between one or more blockchains and their end-user base.

Alternatively, with DEXs, customers generally do not need to transfer their crypto into a centrally managed exchange account. Trading can take place directly from the customer's own wallet, most commonly facilitated via smart contracts.

Once we step away from the distinction between CEX and DEX, there are several mechanisms to bring together demand and supply for a given asset. Most obviously, many crypto exchanges will operate an order book. Users submit orders specifying the price at which they wish to purchase or sell the relevant asset. When compatible buy and sell orders are available, the exchange can match them and execute a trade.

A second approach is seen on many DEXs, where an AMM is employed. Liquidity pools comprise crypto assets deposited into smart contracts. When a user wishes to transact against these, they interact with the pool, at a price dictated by a mathematical function and the available liquidity.

Similar to FX, crypto is quoted in terms of a pair. For example, if someone buys the BTC/USDT pair, they will receive BTC and pay in USDT. BTC is the base currency and USDT is the quote currency, meaning the pair's price expresses how much USDT is required to purchase one BTC. Once a customer understands the composition of a trading pair, they will know what currency they are acquiring, giving up and at what price.

Finally, we must distinguish how a trade will be settled. CEXs typically maintain internal ledgers of their customers' holdings and execute trades without recording each transaction on the blockchain. On-chain transfers generally occur when assets enter or leave the exchange, while trades within the platform can be processed internally. On many DEXs, trades are executed and settled through smart contracts on the relevant blockchain, although parts of the order-matching or routing process may happen off-chain. The former approach will therefore tend to offer greater speed, whereas on-chain settlement is subject to the throughput and cost of the underlying blockchain.

Three common order types form the basis of the language used by crypto traders. A 'market' order instructs the platform to buy or sell immediately at the best available prices, although the final execution price will depend on available liquidity. With a 'limit' order, the trader specifies the maximum price they are willing to pay or the minimum price they will accept. Finally, a 'stop' order triggers another order once a certain price threshold is reached, although this does not guarantee execution at the trigger price.

There are further terms that traders will come across to denote their typical style of trading, such as 'scalping', 'swing' or 'buy and hold'. Again, these are simply descriptive and should not be construed as prescriptive.

A natural extension of the discussion above is that customers can take long or short positions on a crypto asset. Going long means taking a position that benefits if the asset appreciates in value, often by purchasing it directly. Conversely, a short position enables a trader to profit from a decline in the asset's price, although losses can arise if the price moves in the opposite direction.

By using borrowed funds or margin, a customer can increase their exposure beyond the capital they initially commit. While this can lead to greater returns, it also magnifies potential losses. Perpetual futures ('perps') are another product designed to allow traders to take exposure to the future price movements of an asset without a fixed expiry date. These use periodic funding payments between long and short positions to help keep contract prices aligned with the underlying market. Depending on the funding rate and their position, traders may either pay or receive funding.

If a large proportion of the market is exposed to high levels of leverage, the likelihood of forced liquidations can increase during sharp price movements. In turn, the buying or selling triggered by these events may place further upward or downward pressure on the market, potentially creating a liquidation cascade. Futures and options can provide a degree of protection when used to hedge existing exposures (and can of course be used to increase speculative exposure). However, they too carry considerable risk.

It will be apparent from the preceding discussion that customers require access to sufficient liquidity in order to efficiently enter and exit positions. On CEXs, market makers play an important role by submitting buy and sell orders, helping to maintain liquidity and reduce spreads. Similarly, many DEXs depend upon third parties supplying crypto to their liquidity pools, in return for a share of the trading fees generated.

There are a number of further considerations relating to the operation of crypto markets. Some of the more prominent forms of market manipulation are:

And finally, there are a number of other actors and entities that play a part in the crypto market: crypto custodians, information aggregators, government and supervisory authorities, and ETF issuers.

Finally, we touch upon some of the ways in which crypto businesses can secure finance. As with any industry, venture capital (VC) and private equity (PE) firms can invest in crypto-related ventures and provide a range of services beyond pure capital injection. Furthermore, there has been significant innovation in how crypto-native businesses can access funding. The sale of a project's native token(s) can occur via an ICO, allowing it to raise capital through token distribution. The advent of DEXs and CEXs has also enabled IDOs and IEOs respectively. In some cases, groups of investors can coalesce to form a DAO to collectively raise and deploy funds.

There are a number of key elements to understand in order to navigate the crypto market, spanning the range of venues, execution and settlement mechanisms, market actors and financial products.

Both CEXs and DEXs are capable of supporting customers, but differ materially in respect of custody and transparency.

Order books match compatible buy and sell orders, while AMMs use liquidity pools and algorithms to determine trading prices.

The decision to settle trades on- vs. off-chain will have material implications for customers.

Customers can use borrowing or derivatives to build larger positions, and the prevalence of leveraged exposure can create feedback loops throughout the market.

A diverse set of organizations underpin the crypto market, and will continue to evolve over time.

Lastly, the range of fundraising avenues open to crypto businesses also warrants careful consideration.

Market structure: The various mechanisms, market actors, products, rules and economic incentives governing the trading and pricing of an asset.

Centralized Exchange (CEX): A platform that facilitates trading and will typically hold customer assets or balances in custodial accounts.

Decentralized Exchange (DEX): A platform or protocol that enables customers to conduct trades directly from their wallets, commonly through smart contracts.

Order Book: Records the current set of outstanding bids and offers, allowing compatible buy and sell orders to be matched.

Bid: The price a buyer is willing to pay for an asset.

Offer: The price a seller is willing to accept for an asset.

Automated Market Maker (AMM): Allows trading against a pool of assets, with prices determined by a predefined algorithm.

Liquidity: The capacity to transact in an asset without materially affecting its price.

Slippage: The extent to which a trade's execution price differs from the anticipated price.

Settlement: The process of completing a trade and transferring or recording the resulting asset ownership or balances.

Leverage: The use of borrowed funds or derivatives to increase a customer's market exposure relative to their committed capital.

Perpetual Future: A futures-style instrument that does not have a fixed maturity. Generally uses periodic funding payments to help align its price with the underlying market.

Funding Rate: The rate used to calculate periodic payments between long and short positions in perpetual futures markets. Depending on the rate, either side may pay or receive funding.

Liquidation: The forced closing or reduction of a leveraged position when its available margin or collateral falls below the required threshold.

Market Maker: A firm or entity that provides buy and sell quotes to a market, helping maintain liquidity.

Initial Coin Offering (ICO): A fundraising mechanism through which a project offers tokens to participants in exchange for capital.

Decentralized Autonomous Organization (DAO): A structure allowing members to take collective decisions based on governance rules, which may include token-weighted voting.

Crypto market structure is the set of venues, participants, tools, settlement systems, and incentives that determine how digital assets are traded and priced.

A CEX is an intermediary platform that usually holds user balances, while a DEX lets users trade from their own wallets through smart contracts.

An order book lists bids from buyers and asks from sellers. When prices align, a trade can execute.

An AMM is a smart-contract mechanism that lets traders swap against a liquidity pool instead of a traditional order book.

Leverage increases the size of a position using borrowed funds or derivative exposure, which can amplify both gains and losses.

A perpetual future is a derivative contract without a fixed expiration date, usually kept near the spot market through funding payments.

They are crypto-native fundraising models that use token sales or exchange infrastructure to raise capital and distribute tokens.

#4907. Nvidia Reinstates Jensen Huang as CEO Days After Board Ruled Out His Return

Nvidia Reinstates Jensen Huang as CEO Days After Board Ruled Out His Return

Nvidia's board has reinstated Jensen Huang as president and CEO, six days after its chair said directors did not intend to bring him back.

The board voted unanimously to reinstate Huang as president, CEO and a board member, effective immediately, the company said on Monday. It followed "a series of discussions and meetings" with Huang, after which the board was satisfied with his "candor and ability to lead" the firm.

You can now act on the news you read: Go long or short Nvidia with perpetual futures, all from your Decrypt Money Account.

In reaching its decision, the board said it received input from "senior levels of the United States government," and based on that input, it is confident that Huang's reinstatement "poses no national security risk." The statement did not name the officials involved.

"The Board believes Jensen is the right person to lead NVIDIA, and that his reinstatement is in the best interests of our stockholders, employees, partners and customers," board chair Harvey Jones said. Jones will remain chair, and Colette Kress, who served as interim CEO, continues as chief financial officer.

NVIDIA Board reinstates Jensen Huang as President, CEO and Board Director.

Read the release: https://t.co/x4bnjiSVil

— NVIDIA Newsroom (@nvidianewsroom) November 23, 2026

"I take this responsibility with the greatest humility and renewed commitment," Huang said in the statement. "I can't wait to get back to work."

The decision overturns the board's position from last week. "The Nvidia board does not intend to reinstate Jensen as CEO," Jones said on the company's November 17 earnings call, as Nvidia hired executive search firm Heidrick & Struggles to find a permanent replacement.

Hours earlier, Huang had offered to return if the board decided it was in the best interest of shareholders, employees, the company "and America." His comeback had drawn support from President Donald Trump and Elon Musk, even as CNBC reported that directors were not considering it.

Huang resigned on November 12 after reports of extramarital relationships, including one with Alice Huang, a former executive at Singapore-based Nvidia customer Megaspeed whom U.S. officials suspected of being a Chinese intelligence asset. China has denied that she is a spy.

The independent directors' committee investigating whether Huang was the target of a foreign intelligence effort "will proceed to conclusion," Nvidia said, and Huang has said he will cooperate with it.

The company also pointed to its new National Security and Export Control Committee, made up of independent directors, and said it is searching for a chief compliance officer to oversee compliance across the company. Nvidia said it will keep cooperating with government investigations and inquiries.

Huang still faces scrutiny in Washington. House committees have asked him to sit for a closed-door interview on December 1, and Senate Banking Committee Chairman Tim Scott (R-SC) has asked him to testify at a public hearing on December 3.

Nvidia shares rose to over $160 in premarket trading on Monday, up about 28% from Friday's close of $125.53, according to Yahoo! Finance. That would add roughly $780 billion to the company's market value, but still leave the stock below its $166.19 close on the day Huang resigned.

#4906. Ethereum treasury firm BTCS sells $43.8 million in ETH to cut Aave debt, CEO says ‘we do not take this lightly’

Looking for institutional-grade crypto trading? Discover LMAX Digital, the regulated exchange from LMAX Group

The repayment leaves the company holding about 24,245 ETH, alongside $17.9 million in convertible notes due in 2027.

BTCS sold about 27,300 ETH for $43.8 million on Nov. 20 and used the proceeds to repay the same amount of borrowing on Aave, the company said in a Form 8-K filed with the U.S. Securities and Exchange Commission on Monday.

The sale implies an average price of roughly $1,604 per ETH. It came as the world's second-largest crypto asset by market cap slid about 12% from its intraday high to $1,561 on Nov. 20, when Bitcoin Bitcoin (BTC) fell below $60,000 for the first time since July, and the Nasdaq Composite dropped 5.3%.

"Friday was a hard day for the markets and for BTCS," Charles Allen said in a statement. "As ETH fell, we chose to sell ETH and pay down our Aave borrowings rather than carry that debt through a falling market. Selling at these prices came at a real cost to the Company and its shareholders, and we do not take that lightly."

The company sold to limit the risk of liquidation and meet obligations under its senior secured convertible notes, Allen said, adding that the measures would put BTCS on a more durable financial footing.

After the latest sale, BTCS estimated it held about 24,245 ETH and cash and digital assets worth about $61 million, based on an ETH price of $1,722 on Nov. 22.

The company also had about $17.9 million of senior secured convertible notes outstanding, with maturities in May and July 2027.

BTCS temporarily pulled its Imperium DeFi business out of liquidity pools during the volatility. The company said the capital earns no liquidity-pool fees while undeployed and that it intends to redeploy it when conditions improve.

Imperium generated $3.5 million of revenue in the third quarter, accounting for about 86% of BTCS’s $4.1 million in total revenue.

BTCS shares fell 6.26% on Monday, extending a 77.41% year-to-date decline. Ethereum has declined 28.16% over the past month and 42.99% year to date.

Bitcoin joined the party, trading near $63,500 after dipping below $60,000 during Friday’s selloff. Ethereum climbed to about $1,790, and cash CFDs tracking the Nasdaq 100 and S&P 500 rebounded to roughly 26,950 and 7,285, respectively.

The catalyst was Nvidia’s announcement that its founder Jensen Huang had been reinstated as president, CEO and director, effective immediately. The board voted unanimously just six days after publicly ruling out his return—and even doubling down on their decision several times.

Huang resigned November 12 amid reports of extramarital relationships, including one with a businesswoman U.S. officials suspected of ties to Chinese intelligence. Beijing has denied the espionage allegation, and no public evidence has established that Huang knowingly passed company secrets to China.

Colette Kress, Nvidia’s finance chief, took over as interim CEO while the company launched a search for a permanent replacement. On November 17, board chair Harvey Jones said directors did not intend to reinstate Huang, despite a campaign for his return backed by Silicon Valley executives and President Donald Trump.

Monday’s reversal followed meetings with Huang and input from senior U.S. government officials. The board said it was satisfied with his candor and leadership ability and was confident his return posed “no national security risk,” though its independent investigation will continue.

“I can’t wait to get back to work,” Huang said in the statement. Kress will remain chief financial officer, and Jones will stay on as board chair.

“It tells us to some extent that Jensen Huang was too big to be fired,” Interactive Brokers strategist Steve Sosnick told Reuters.

Prediction markets were caught off guard, too. A Polymarket contract on Huang rejoining Nvidia by November 30 traded near 99% after the announcement, compared with roughly 3% shortly beforehand.

His return also tanked the probabilities of the AI bubble bursting. After his outsting, Polymarket odds skyrocketed to more than 70%, minutes after his reinstatement, the odds dropped to 14%.

The rally followed an ugly stretch for AI stocks. Nvidia closed Friday at $125.53, about 47.5% below its October high, while the Nasdaq lost roughly 10% over the previous week. Bitcoin fell toward $55,100 Friday night before staging a weekend recovery.

Monday’s bounce pushed Nvidia above the $166.19 closing price recorded on the day Huang resigned. Bitcoin, meanwhile, recovered the $63,000 area, but its daily chart still shows a bearish moving-average configuration and a relative strength index near 34, indicating that the recent relief rally has not erased the broader downtrend.

Overall, crypto traders are still timid but evidently don’t think this is the end of the world.

On the chart, Bitcoin faces initial resistance around $65,030, followed by $68,090. On the downside, $61,240 and the psychological $60,000 mark are immediate levels to watch; another break lower would put the recent $55,100 area back in focus.

One of the few notable losers was Anthropic, whose stock slipped 3.16% to $85.81. That left the Claude developer about 25% below its post-IPO peak near $115, although still slightly above the $83 offering price set for its $81.34 billion public offering last Thursday. Nvidia itself committed about $10 billion to a separate, conditional private investment in Anthropic alongside the IPO.

The decline looks more like investors continuing to digest a pricey, volatile listing than a reaction to Huang’s reinstatement. But the internet has another theory: memes and posts have cast Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei as playing a role in Huang’s ouster because of his support towards open-weight models and his decision to buy Hugging Face, the world’s largest repository of open source AI models, to protect the ecosystem.

Huang championed broad access to open models, while Amodei has argued for tighter safeguards around powerful AI systems, especially warning against open source AI competing against close models like the ones his company develops, a position that has been widely criticized by influential figures in the AI scene like Yan Lecun who called his mindset “a new form of medieval obscurantism.”

Nvidia’s independent inquiry into the reported foreign intelligence effort remains open. Huang has also been asked to meet House investigators on December 1 and testify before a Senate panel on December 3.

#4897. Coldcard Postmortem Says Weak Seeds, Not Hacked Devices, Drove Bitcoin Thefts

Coinkite on Tuesday published its full postmortem on the Coldcard seed-generation flaw that let thieves drain bitcoin from customer wallets starting in July, saying no device was hacked and that the stolen keys were rebuilt offline from weak seeds.

The 18-page report, dated Nov. 23 and modeled on a National Transportation Safety Board accident report, lays out how the defect shipped in Coldcard firmware from March 29, 2021, through July 30, 2026, and why years of outside reviews missed it.

“The losses are real and, for some customers, life-changing. No report or firmware update can undo that. We are sorry,” Coinkite wrote.

A seed is the list of recovery words that controls a bitcoin wallet, and it is only as safe as the randomness used to create it. Coldcard devices were supposed to draw that randomness from the hardware random number generator built into their STM32 chip.

Instead, a firmware setting switched that hardware source off, and a safeguard in Coinkite’s libNgU code library failed to catch it. Seed generation quietly fell back to Yasmarang, a predictable software generator built into MicroPython, the programming environment the firmware runs on.

Nothing crashed, and the devices produced normal-looking seed words. Coinkite estimates affected seeds carried roughly 40 bits of effective security on the older Mk2 and Mk3 models and about 72 bits on the Mk4, Mk5 and Q, against an intended 128 bits. That shrinks the pool of possible seeds enough for attackers to search it offline.

The report says Coinkite’s release checks confirmed the hardware code was present, but never confirmed that seed generation actually reached it. At least 15 independent review efforts since 2021 also missed the flaw, including two paid third-party reviews and an AI-assisted firmware review this year that produced 85 candidate findings.

Unexpected transactions from affected seeds began July 29. Coinkite said it identified the defect the next day, after users discovered thefts, and shipped fixed firmware for every supported release track on July 31.

As of Nov. 18, Coinkite had received about 300 loss-related support tickets tied to 242 customer accounts, or about 0.21% of its estimated Coldcard user base. The company’s blog post cites 236 accounts. Because Coldcard is self-custodial, Coinkite can only count losses that customers report, and it says the true number is likely higher.

The report cites Galaxy Research figures showing 1,778.84 BTC stolen from more than 8,600 addresses, worth about $107 million at today’s price. Galaxy pegged losses above $115 million in August, based on prices when the coins were taken, and white hats later moved some exposed coins into a recovery trust.

Who found and exploited the flaw is still unknown, and law enforcement is investigating. The report calls AI-assisted discovery “a plausible hypothesis, not an attribution,” noting that the first thefts came two days after the full model weights of the AI model Kimi K3 were released. Bitcoin Core developers ended long embargoes last month for bugs that AI tools can easily rediscover.

Coinkite said an independent review by Keylabs, published Oct. 15, found the defect “fully closed” in Mk5 firmware 5.6.2 and 5.6.3 and Q firmware 1.5.2Q and 1.5.3Q. That review did not cover Coldcard’s Edge releases, a preview track for developers and early adopters.

Newer Coldcard firmware now requires users to add their own randomness, through key presses, dice rolls or coin flips, and mixes it with three hardware sources. The device also checks at startup that seed generation reaches the hardware generator, and stops if it does not.

But a firmware update does not repair a seed that was already created on affected firmware. Coinkite told owners whose seeds were made on affected firmware to install verified fixed firmware, create a new seed and move their coins. Seeds made with at least 50 private dice rolls were not weakened.

Three of the report’s 15 recommendations to Coinkite remain open, including whether to compensate affected customers. The company said it has “no decision” on a plan yet and asked whoever holds the stolen bitcoin to return it through [email protected].

#4891. Anchorage Digital Sets Up Asset Manager to Offer Bitcoin Yield to Clients

Anchorage Digital, the first federally chartered crypto bank in the U.S., is moving into asset management with a new subsidiary that will offer custody clients a way to earn yield on their bitcoin.

The unit, called 61st Parallel Asset Management, is expected to start operating by early December, CEO Nathan McCauley said in an interview to CoinDesk. Its first product will be a bitcoin-denominated fund, meaning returns are measured in BTC rather than dollars. The name nods to the city of Anchorage, Alaska, which sits at 61 degrees north latitude.

“We have increasingly heard clients say they want to earn on top of the assets they hold at Anchorage — something that’s very common among the large financial institutions of the world,” McCauley said.

Anchorage has filed a Form ADV, the disclosure document investment advisers use to register with the Securities and Exchange Commission or state regulators, or to report as exempt advisers. The form covers a firm’s ownership, business, assets under management, fees and conflicts of interest. As of Tuesday afternoon, the SEC’s public adviser database showed no record for 61st Parallel, so the filing’s details were not yet public.

The entity itself is not new. New York state records show that 61st Parallel Asset Management LLC, a Delaware company, registered to do business in New York on July 8, listing an office on Park Avenue South in Manhattan.

Anchorage already lets clients earn on some holdings. Its website lists staking, which pays rewards for helping secure proof-of-stake networks, and a separate rewards product for eligible assets. Bitcoin runs on proof-of-work and cannot be staked natively.

Anchorage has not said publicly how the fund will generate yield, what it will charge or which clients will qualify. Those details matter to bitcoin holders, because bitcoin pays no interest on its own. Common ways to earn on it include lending coins out, posting them as collateral or selling options against them, and each carries its own risk.

Public companies have already tested some of those approaches. Trump Media disclosed this month that it had pledged about 73% of its bitcoin to an options program in which the counterparty can rehypothecate, or reuse, the coins.

Founded in 2017, Anchorage received a national trust bank charter from the Office of the Comptroller of the Currency in January 2021, the first crypto firm to win one. The OCC lifted a 2022 consent order over the bank’s anti-money laundering controls in August 2025.

The bank no longer stands alone. Last December, the OCC granted conditional approvals to five more digital asset firms, including Circle, Ripple, BitGo, Paxos and Fidelity Digital Assets, to become national trust banks.

The asset manager is the latest in a run of expansions. On Nov. 5, Anchorage Digital Swap Dealer LLC applied to the National Futures Association to register as a swap dealer with the Commodity Futures Trading Commission. The company said much of its options growth has come from public companies holding bitcoin and ether on their balance sheets.

In February, Tether made a $100 million strategic investment in Anchorage at a $4.2 billion valuation, after picking Anchorage Digital Bank as the issuer of its U.S. stablecoin. Anchorage also ran its first employee tender offer at that valuation instead of raising new primary capital.

In June, the company rolled out off-exchange settlement with Binance, letting institutions trade on the exchange while their assets stay in segregated custody at the bank. Anchorage also offers trading, staking and settlement to institutional clients.

The swap dealer application remains under review by the National Futures Association, and McCauley said at the time that the company was not in a position to speculate on timing.
